study.title: Leviticus 18 - Sexual Holiness and Separation of the practices of nations
study.overview: Leviticus 18 presents a divine order that calls Israel to live differently from Egypt and Canaan. The chapter brings together prohibitions on incest, adultery, illicit sexual relations, child sacrifice to Molach, homosexual relations and bestiality, and concludes with a solemn warning: the very land rejects moral impurity. The text does not only deal with social rules; it places the sexuality, worship, and identity of the people under the authority of the Lord, which requires obedience because it is the God of covenant.

outline.title: Called to distinct obedience
outline.explanation: The chapter begins and ends with the same statement of authority: the Lord is the God of Israel. The people must not imitate the customs of Egypt or Canaan, but to walk in the divine statutes, because true life is linked to obedience to the covenant.

outline.title: Prohibitions against sexual sin and the breaking of family order
outline.explanation: Most of the chapter details forbidden unions: close relatives, sister-in-law and daughter-in-law, adultery, relationships with women in menstrual impurity and sexual union outside the marriage bond. The focus is to preserve the honor of the family, the conjugal fidelity and the purity of the people.

outline.title: Ivory impurity and judgment on abominations
outline.explanation: The text goes from the family scope to worship: it prohibits surrendering descent to Moloque and condemns practices that are called abominations, including sexual relations contrary to the created order. The nations have been expelled for these sins, and Israel is warned that the land will also reject it if such practices are repeated.

study.context: According to the notes, chapters 18 and 20 deal mainly with sexual matters, in contrast to pagan practices, and function as a frame for the call to the holiness of Leviticus 19. The language of covenant in "I am the Lord your God" reminds the authority of the great King over the people. The notes also point out that the list of prohibitions protects the house, family and moral order, and that the judgment on Canaan serves as a historical warning to Israel.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter states that holiness is not an abstract idea, but concrete obedience to the God of the covenant. The body, marriage, family and worship belong to the Lord and cannot be shaped by the standards of the nations. The text unites morality and cult: disorderly sexual practices and idolatry appear side by side as forms of contamination. There is also a community and territorial dimension: sin is not only individual, but pollutes the land and threatens the permanence of the people in it. In evangelical reading, this shows that God's grace does not nullify its requirement of purity; rather, it calls the redeemed people to reflect the character of the holy God.

scholarViews.insight: The repetition of "I am the Lord your God" framed the chapter as a language of covenant and authority, demanding an obedient response from the people.
The laws of the chapter cover the seventh commandment and remain morally binding, as they deal with duties rooted in the very light of nature.
The final order shows that preservation against false worship depends on seriously observing the statutes of the true God.

questions: In what ways does the culture around us try to normalize what Leviticus 18 calls abomination?
How does the repetition of "I am the Lord" changes the way we read these prohibitions: as cold rules or as a covenant of belonging?
In which areas of Christian life today do we need to distinguish clearly between biblical holiness and customs accepted by society?
study.practice: Read the chapter as a call to examine habits, relationships, and entertainment in the light of God's holiness. Reject any practice that normalizes sexual impurity, infidelity, exploitation of the body or mixes between true worship and idolatry. In the Christian context, this means cultivating fidelity in marriage, purity in thinking and acting, and courage to live differently from culture, without arrogance, but with fear of the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not explain all the details of each prohibition nor do they discuss in depth the exact range of some expressions, such as the punishment mentioned for certain practices. There is also not enough basis here to state with certainty more than the text and notes say about old custom, specific forms of idolatry or possible legal exceptions beyond what was explicitly indicated.
